questions.q: What was the central idea of Ebright's theory on how cells work, as described in the chapter?
questions.a: Ebright's theory proposed that cells read their DNA blueprint by copying it into RNA, which then directs the building of proteins — essentially explaining the flow of genetic information (DNA → RNA → protein). A wrong answer (e.g., "he discovered the structure of DNA" or "he proved cells divide") reveals the student confuses his theory with other famous discoveries or hasn't read the specific description in the text.

questions.q: Why was the publication of this theory at age 22 considered a remarkable achievement in the context of Ebright's journey?
questions.a: It was remarkable because it came from a young scientist who had been building toward it since childhood — starting with butterfly collecting, then the gold spots discovery, and finally solving a fundamental biological problem. A wrong answer focusing only on his age ("he was young") misses the narrative arc: the theory was the result of years of curiosity, failed experiments, and incremental learning, not a one-time stroke of genius.

questions.q: How does Ebright's theory demonstrate the application of the scientific method? Use one example from his earlier work to support your answer.
questions.a: Ebright observed gold spots on monarch pupae (observation), hypothesized they produced a hormone (hypothesis), experimented with extracting and testing the hormone (experiment), and used those results to build his broader theory on cell function (conclusion/theory building). A wrong answer that lists scientific method steps without linking to his actual work shows mechanical recall without textual application.

questions.q: Analyze how the theory connects to the chapter's title "The Making of a Scientist". What does this moment reveal about the "making" process?
questions.a: The theory shows that a scientist is "made" through sustained curiosity, learning from failures (like the failed science fair projects), mentorship (mother, Dr. Urquhart), and connecting small discoveries to big questions. A wrong answer that says "it proves he was smart" ignores the process-oriented theme — the chapter emphasizes journey over innate talent.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Ebright's theory on cell function was his most important contribution because it was published in a top journal." Defend or challenge using evidence from the text.
questions.a: Challenge: The text emphasizes that his *process* — asking questions, experimenting, persisting — matters more than any single publication. The theory was a milestone, but the "making" continued. A wrong answer that agrees solely because of the journal prestige misses the author's message: scientific greatness lies in the habit of inquiry, not accolades.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from Ebright's perspective on the day his theory was published, capturing his scientific mindset (not just emotions).
questions.a: A strong entry includes: reference to the DNA-RNA-protein idea, mention of a past failure or question that led here, and a forward-looking question (e.g., "Now I wonder how RNA knows where to go..."). A poor entry focuses only on pride or fame, showing the student hasn't internalized the scientific temperament the chapter celebrates.
